section.title: Lessons from Israel's History
section.sectionRationale: This long Asaphite maskil opens Book III's meditation on covenant history. Asaph turns Israel's wilderness story into a parable so the next generation will not repeat their fathers' forgetfulness, then traces God's history of patience through repeated rebellion to His sovereign choice of Judah, Zion, and David, the shepherd king.
section.thesis: Though Israel forgot God's wonders again and again and tested Him in the wilderness and in the land, God's compassion held back His full wrath, and His sovereign choice of David the shepherd king previews the greater Son of David who will shepherd His people forever.
section.frameNote: Eight units carry the history in order: the call to teach the next generation, 1-8; Ephraim's failure and God's wonders at the Exodus, 9-16; testing God for bread and meat, 17-31; shallow repentance and real compassion, 32-39; the plagues on Egypt, 40-51; led like a flock into the land, 52-55; rebellion in the land and the loss of Shiloh, 56-64; and God's choice of Judah, Zion, and David, 65-72.

verses.text: Give ear, O my people, to my instruction; listen to the words of my mouth.
I will open my mouth in {{mashal|parables}}; I will utter things hidden from the beginning,
that we have heard and known and our fathers have relayed to us.
We will not hide them from their children but will declare to the next generation the praises of the LORD and His might and the wonders He has performed.
For He established a testimony in Jacob and appointed a law in Israel, which He commanded our fathers to teach to their children,
that the coming generation would know them, even children yet to be born, to arise and tell their own children
that they should put their confidence in God, not forgetting His works, but keeping His commandments.
Then they will not be like their fathers, a stubborn and {{marah|rebellious}} generation, whose heart was not loyal, whose spirit was not faithful to God.
The archers of Ephraim turned back on the day of battle.
They failed to keep God's covenant and refused to live by His law.
They forgot what He had done, the wonders He had shown them.
He worked wonders before their fathers in the land of Egypt, in the region of Zoan.
He split the sea and brought them through; He set the waters upright like a wall.
He led them with a cloud by day and with a light of fire all night.
He split the rocks in the wilderness and gave them drink as abundant as the seas.
He brought streams from the stone and made water flow down like rivers.

units.label: Testing God for bread and meat

verses.text: But they continued to sin against Him, rebelling in the desert against the Most High.
They willfully {{nasah|tested}} God by demanding the food they craved.
They spoke against God, saying, "Can God really prepare a table in the wilderness?
When He struck the rock, water gushed out and torrents raged. But can He also give bread or supply His people with meat?"
Therefore the LORD heard and was filled with wrath; so a fire was kindled against Jacob, and His anger flared against Israel,
because they did not believe God or rely on His salvation.
Yet He commanded the clouds above and opened the doors of the heavens.
He rained down manna for them to eat; He gave them grain from heaven.
Man ate the bread of angels; He sent them food in abundance.
He stirred the east wind from the heavens and drove the south wind by His might.
He rained meat on them like dust, and winged birds like the sand of the sea.
He felled them in the midst of their camp, all around their dwellings.
So they ate and were well filled, for He gave them what they craved.
Yet before they had filled their desire, with the food still in their mouths,
God's anger flared against them, and He put to death their strongest and subdued the young men of Israel.

units.label: Shallow repentance, real compassion
units.note: God remembers they are but flesh

verses.text: In spite of all this, they kept on sinning; despite His wonderful works, they did not believe.
So He ended their days in futility, and their years in sudden terror.
When He slew them, they would seek Him; they repented and searched for God.
And they remembered that God was their Rock, that God Most High was their Redeemer.
But they deceived Him with their mouths, and lied to Him with their tongues.
Their hearts were disloyal to Him, and they were unfaithful to His covenant.
And yet He was compassionate; He forgave their iniquity and did not destroy them. He often restrained His anger and did not unleash His full wrath.
He remembered that they were but flesh, a passing breeze that does not return.
How often they disobeyed Him in the wilderness and grieved Him in the desert!
Again and again they tested God and provoked the Holy One of Israel.
They did not remember His power, the day He redeemed them from the adversary,
when He performed His signs in Egypt and His wonders in the fields of Zoan.
He turned their rivers to blood, and from their streams they could not drink.
He sent swarms of flies that devoured them, and frogs that devastated them.
He gave their crops to the grasshopper, the fruit of their labor to the locust.
He killed their vines with hailstones and their sycamore-figs with sleet.
He abandoned their cattle to the hail and their livestock to bolts of lightning.
He unleashed His fury against them, wrath, indignation, and calamity, a band of destroying angels.
He cleared a path for His anger; He did not spare them from death but delivered their lives to the plague.
He struck all the firstborn of Egypt, the virility in the tents of Ham.

units.label: Led like a flock into the land

verses.text: He led out His people like sheep and guided them like a flock in the wilderness.
He led them safely, so they did not fear, but the sea engulfed their enemies.
He brought them to His holy land, to the mountain His right hand had acquired.
He drove out nations before them and apportioned their inheritance; He settled the tribes of Israel in their tents.

units.label: Rebellion in the land, loss of Shiloh

verses.text: But they tested and disobeyed God Most High, for they did not keep His decrees.
They turned back and were faithless like their fathers, twisted like a faulty bow.
They enraged Him with their high places and provoked His jealousy with their idols.
On hearing it, God was furious and rejected Israel completely.
He abandoned the tabernacle of Shiloh, the tent He had pitched among men.
He delivered His strength to captivity, and His splendor to the hand of the adversary.
He surrendered His people to the sword because He was enraged by His heritage.
Fire consumed His young men, and their maidens were left without wedding songs.
His priests fell by the sword, but their widows could not lament.

units.label: God's choice of Judah, Zion, and David
units.note: shepherd king after God's own heart

verses.text: Then the Lord awoke as from sleep, like a mighty warrior overcome by wine.
He beat back His foes; He put them to everlasting shame.
He rejected the tent of Joseph and refused the tribe of Ephraim.
But He {{bachar|chose}} the tribe of Judah, Mount Zion, which He loved.
He built His sanctuary like the heights, like the earth He has established forever.
He chose David His servant and took him from the sheepfolds;
from tending the ewes He brought him to be {{raah|shepherd}} of His people Jacob, of Israel His inheritance.
So David shepherded them with integrity of heart and guided them with skillful hands.

mashal.gloss: A parable, proverb, or extended comparison teaching wisdom through story. Asaph will not merely list facts but shape Israel's history into a parable so it lands on the heart; Matthew 13:35 applies this very verse to Jesus' teaching in parables.

marah.gloss: To be rebellious, defiant, or bitter against authority. Naming the fathers 'a stubborn and rebellious generation' identifies the deep pattern beneath every failure that follows in the psalm.

nasah.gloss: To test or try. Israel tested God, demanding proof of His care even after seeing His wonders, turning the tables on who was really on trial in the wilderness.

bachar.gloss: To choose or elect. God rejected the tent of Joseph but chose the tribe of Judah, Mount Zion, and David, a sovereign, gracious election that runs forward to the greater Son of David.

raah.gloss: To shepherd, tend, or pasture. David is taken from tending ewes to shepherd God's people, the same verb used of God's own care for Israel like a flock, joining king and God in one image fulfilled in Christ, the Good Shepherd.

basic.context: Asaph turns Israel's whole wilderness history into a long parable so that the next generation will hope in God and not repeat their fathers' pattern. Again and again God works wonders, Israel forgets and rebels, judgment falls, and yet God's compassion holds back His full wrath. The psalm ends by tracing God's sovereign move away from failed Ephraim to His chosen king, David, a humble shepherd raised up to shepherd God's own flock.
basic.hermeneutics: This is real history told for a pastoral purpose, to instruct the generation being taught rather than merely to record facts. The refrain 'they forgot, yet He remembered' is the psalm's engine; each rebellion and each act of divine patience is meant to be heard and applied, not simply observed.
basic.originalLanguages: Asaph calls his song a mashal, a parable, the very word Matthew 13:35 quotes to explain why Jesus taught in parables. He names Israel's sin marah, rebellious, and their provocation nasah, testing God. At the end God bachar, chooses, Judah and David, whom He sets to raah, shepherd, His people, language that flows straight into Christ.
basic.typology: The manna, bread from heaven that still left Israel hungry and unbelieving, points to Jesus, the true bread of life, John 6:31-35. David, taken from the sheepfolds to shepherd Israel, previews Christ, the great Son of David and the Good Shepherd who will not fail as Israel's kings and generations did.
basic.christ: Matthew 13:34-35 cites Psalm 78:2 directly, 'I will open my mouth in parables,' as the reason Jesus taught in parables, showing the psalm itself pointing to Christ's teaching ministry. The psalm's climax, God choosing David the shepherd, anticipates Jesus, the Son of David who shepherds His people with perfect integrity, John 10:11.
basic.god: God is patient almost past belief, forgiving Israel's shallow, repeated unfaithfulness and remembering that they are but flesh, yet He is also just, letting real consequences fall on persistent rebellion, from wilderness plagues on the disobedient to the loss of Shiloh. His sovereign choice of Judah and David shows He is free to redirect history according to His own grace.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 13:34-35 quotes this psalm's opening as the reason Jesus taught in parables. John 6:31-35 shows Jesus as the true bread from heaven that the manna only foreshadowed. 1 Corinthians 10:1-11 uses this same wilderness history as a warning to the church. John 10:11 shows Jesus as the Good Shepherd David's kingship anticipated.
basic.oneStory: This psalm rehearses Israel's history precisely so hope in God will survive to the next generation. Its pattern of forgetting and mercy, judgment and patience, runs all the way to God's choice of David the shepherd, and from David the story runs on to Jesus, the greater Shepherd and Son of David who teaches in parables and never forgets His flock.

context.literary:
Psalm 78 is the second longest psalm in the Psalter, after Psalm 119, and its shape is easy to lose in the flood of detail. A prologue of eight verses, 1-8, states the method and the aim. Then two great sweeps of history follow, each running from rescue to rebellion to judgment. The first, verses 12-39, walks through the wilderness: sea, cloud and water from the rock, then craving, quail, and a sham repentance. The second, verses 40-64, starts again from Egypt and carries the story into the land, ending at the loss of Shiloh. Verses 65-72 break the pattern and turn upward to Judah, Zion and David.

The psalm runs on repeated words. Wonders open the prologue, verse 4, and return at verses 11, 12, 32 and 43, always in the same tension: the wonders are done and then forgotten. Testing and rebelling recur, verses 17, 18, 40, 41 and 56, and the plain phrase 'again and again,' verse 41, names the rhythm of the whole. Against that, God's actions are listed in tight strings of verbs: He split, led, gave, rained, felled. Israel, by contrast, mostly speaks in complaint, and the only direct speech from the people is the sneer of verses 19-20.

Two frames enclose the middle. Ephraim is the subject at verse 9 and again at verse 67, so the rejection of Ephraim answers the first mention of its failure. The flock image shapes the other frame: God led out His people 'like sheep,' verse 52, and at the end He sets David to shepherd them, verses 70-72. The whole history is read as the story of a flock and a shepherd.

Note two silences. Moses is never named in the psalm, so all the action belongs to God. And the psalm stops with David, without mentioning exile.
context.historical:
The psalm is headed a maskil of Asaph, and the Asaph collection runs through Psalms 73 to 83. The setting depends on how verses 60 to 72 are read. Some place the psalm in the early monarchy, when the memory of the ark's capture was fresh and David's rise still needed explaining. Others place it after the fall of the northern kingdom in 722 BC, when refugees and a reforming Judah could look back on the long story of Ephraim's decline. The text itself gives only the ingredients: Shiloh's fall, the rejection of Joseph's house, and David's shepherd kingship. It does not name the moment, and a reader should be slow to claim more than that.

Shiloh had been the central sanctuary in the hill country of Ephraim, where the tent of meeting was set up after the conquest, Joshua 18:1. When Israel carried the ark out to battle against the Philistines, the ark was captured and thirty thousand foot soldiers fell, 1 Samuel 4:10-11. The ark never went back to Shiloh. Centuries later Jeremiah could point to the ruin of Shiloh as a warning that God does not guarantee any building, Jeremiah 7:12-14 and 26:6.

The region of Zoan, verses 12 and 43, is the eastern Delta of Egypt, named again in Numbers 13:22 and Isaiah 19:11, so the psalm sets the plagues in Pharaoh's home ground. The instruction to tell the children is deeply rooted in Israel's practice: the Passover question, Exodus 12:26-27, the memorial stones at the Jordan, Joshua 4:6-7, and the command to teach children what the eyes had seen, Deuteronomy 4:9. Asaph is doing in song what Israel's fathers did around the table.
context.canonical:
Psalm 78 belongs to a small family of Old Testament retellings of Israel's story: Psalms 105, 106, 135 and 136, Ezekiel 20 and Nehemiah 9. Each has its own slant. Psalm 105 dwells on the gifts; Psalm 106 dwells on the sins, and closes by noting that God 'remembered His covenant with them,' Psalm 106:45. Psalm 78 holds both together and lets the sins and the mercy stand side by side. Nehemiah 9:17 gives the same credal line that Psalm 78:38 reflects, 'gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and rich in loving devotion,' which itself echoes Exodus 34:6.

The psalm also anchors the Asaph sequence around it. Its last word for Israel is God's 'inheritance,' verse 71, and Psalm 79 opens with the nations invading that same inheritance. Psalm 80 then prays to the Shepherd who leads Joseph, and Psalm 81 returns to the wilderness and to Meribah. Read in order, these four psalms move from the history to the crisis it produced.

In the New Testament the psalm is used at three points. Matthew 13:34-35 quotes its opening as the mark of Jesus' teaching. John 6:31 quotes the line 'He gave them bread from heaven to eat,' which is close to Psalm 78:24. And Paul's warning to the Corinthians in 1 Corinthians 10:1-11 follows the psalm's wilderness pattern so closely, with the sea, the cloud, the rock, the craving and the testing, that the two read like a sermon and its text. Stephen's speech in Acts 7 tells the same story of resisting the one who rescues.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Asaph writes as a teacher who is also a hearer. The first person plural in verses 3 and 4 puts him inside the chain: 'we have heard and know,' 'our fathers have relayed to us,' 'we will not hide them from their children.' He is not scolding an outside audience. He is passing on what he received, and he wants the next generation to take the same posture, to arise and tell their own children, verse 6.

His method is honesty. He does not flatter the tribes or airbrush the fathers. The word he chooses for the generation before them is 'stubborn and rebellious,' verse 8, and he tells the story of their failures in detail. The point is not shame but hope. He says the goal is that they would put their confidence in God, not forgetting His works, but keeping His commandments, verse 7. Hope comes from an accurate memory of both what God did and what people did.

He also means his hearers to see where the story leads. The long tale of failure does not end in despair but in a Shepherd King chosen by grace, so that hearers who feel the weight of Ephraim's failure can also hear that God has not run out of ways to lead His flock. Asaph wants them to leave the psalm sobered, humble, grateful, and still expecting God to act.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Most of the psalm is description: what Israel did, what God did in reply. Not every detail can be moved directly onto us. The fire that fell on the camp, verse 21, and the death of the strongest in verse 31 report particular judgments at particular moments, and the psalm does not tell us to expect the same measure in our own days. Nor does it teach that every hardship is a punishment. The book of Job argues against that reading.

What the psalm does prescribe is set out in its opening verses and is meant to hold in every generation. Teach the works of God to children. Do it in the open, without hiding hard chapters. Aim the teaching at trust and obedience, not merely information, verse 7. And hold on to the two truths the history keeps showing: sin is serious and has consequences, and God's compassion outlasts our failures. Paul draws the same line in 1 Corinthians 10:6 and 11, where he says these things 'took place as examples' and 'were written down as warnings for us.' The story is written for imitation in what it commends and for caution in what it condemns.

debates.question: What are 'the archers of Ephraim' who turned back on the day of battle in verse 9?

views.label: A specific defeat, perhaps the loss at Ebenezer and Aphek when the ark was taken
views.case: Verse 9 sits right before the wilderness history and right after a summary of covenant failure. Because the psalm ends with Shiloh, in the tribe of Ephraim, and the loss of the ark, 1 Samuel 4:10-11, some hold that the prologue points ahead to that defeat as the recent example of the pattern.

views.label: A figure for the tribe's general covenant failure, not one recorded battle
views.case: No Old Testament narrative reports Ephraimite archers fleeing in just this way. Verse 10 explains the retreat by unfaithfulness, not by tactics, which suggests the line is a compressed image of Ephraim's whole record, with 'day of battle' standing for any hour when the covenant was tested.

views.label: A reference to an earlier Ephraimite episode that is no longer fully known to us
views.case: The Old Testament preserves scattered notes about Ephraim's military efforts, such as 1 Chronicles 7:20-22, and Asaph's first hearers may have known a story we can only guess at. On this view the honest answer is that the allusion is real but the details are lost.

debates.bearing: Whichever event is meant, the point is stated in verse 10: the collapse was spiritual before it was military. The psalm's lesson does not hang on identifying the battle.

debates.question: Is the psalm's ending a claim for Judah's superiority, or a wider message about grace?

views.label: A Judahite statement legitimating Zion and David against the northern tribes
views.case: Verses 67 to 71 name Ephraim's rejection and Judah's choice in the same breath. After the division of the kingdom, 1 Kings 12:16, a Judahite writer could well have used the psalm to say that the temple in Zion and the house of David alone were God's choices.

views.label: A pastoral warning to every tribe that God's choices are grace and not merit
views.case: Judah's own record in the psalm's world is not spotless, and the psalm gives no reason Judah was chosen except that God 'loved' Zion, verse 68. The election of David is set against the sheepfolds, verse 70, which reads as a lesson in humility. Deuteronomy 7:7-8 makes the same point about Israel as a whole.

debates.bearing: The two readings need not compete. The psalm can honestly present Zion and David as God's chosen place and king while keeping the emphasis on His free choice, not on a tribe's standing.

debates.question: Does verse 65, 'the Lord awoke as from sleep,' imply a real change in God, or is it figurative language for His action?

views.label: A vivid anthropomorphism describing God's sudden, decisive intervention, without implying He was literally inactive or asleep
views.case: Scripture elsewhere insists God neither slumbers nor sleeps, Psalm 121:4, so the image describes how deliverance felt to Israel rather than a change in God's unceasing attention.

views.label: A genuine picture of God's dynamic engagement with history, entering fully into the drama of judgment and rescue
views.case: The psalm's whole narrative shape, wrath rising and mercy responding, takes God's real involvement in time seriously rather than reducing every action to timeless decree.

debates.bearing: Either reading upholds both God's unchanging character and the psalm's confidence that He genuinely acts within Israel's history to save. The image also answers the long silence of verses 59 to 64 with the shout of a rescuer.

study.originalLanguages:
Asaph says he will utter chidot 'from of old,' the BSB's 'things hidden from the beginning,' verse 2. The Hebrew word is the one used for a riddle, as in Samson's riddle at the wedding feast, Judges 14:12-19, and it stands beside the mashal in Proverbs 1:6. A riddle is a saying whose sense is not lying on the surface. Asaph's claim is not that his history is obscure but that the ordinary events of Israel's story hold a hidden meaning, which the parable brings out. Matthew's quotation of the line, 'things hidden since the foundation of the world,' Matthew 13:35, widens that thought from Israel's past to the plan behind creation.

The verse that stops the psalm's despair is verse 38. 'He forgave their iniquity' translates the verb kipper, the ordinary word for making atonement, joined to the word for iniquity, avon. The Lord 'atoned' for their iniquity even as they lied to Him, verses 36-37. The next line adds that He 'often restrained His anger,' literally turned it back again and again, the same pattern as the people's repeated sinning. Jewish tradition counts verse 38 as the middle verse of the Psalter, a small sign of how central the line was felt to be. Nehemiah 9:17 and Exodus 34:6 supply the description of the God who does this, 'gracious and compassionate, slow to anger.'

In verse 39 God 'remembered that they were but flesh, a passing breeze that does not return.' The word for flesh, basar, marks weakness, and the wind that goes and does not come back is the image of a brief life. Verse 25 is rare. The BSB has 'the bread of angels,' from the Hebrew for bread of the mighty ones, a poetic name for manna that the Septuagint reads as angels' food. It is not a claim that angels eat, but a way of saying the manna came from heaven's own store, and John 6:31 connects it to 'bread from heaven.'

In verse 57 Israel is 'twisted like a faulty bow.' The adjective describes a bow that will not shoot true, and Hosea 7:16 uses the same word for the fickle turning of the northern people. The image fits the archers of verse 9 exactly: a weapon that fails when it is drawn.

The verb for God's acquiring in verse 54, that He brought them 'to the mountain His right hand had acquired,' is qanah, the verb Moses used in the Song of the Sea for the people God 'bought,' Exodus 15:16, in a passage that ends with 'the mountain of Your inheritance,' Exodus 15:17. Asaph is quietly saying that the promise sung at the sea has come true.

Finally, David shepherds by two things in verse 72: the integrity of his heart and the skill of his hands. The first is the word tom, wholeness, the same quality claimed for the righteous in Psalm 26:1. The second is the plural of a word for understanding. Character and competence are named together, as the two things a shepherd needs.

typology.type: The rock split in the wilderness, Psalm 78:15-16, 20
typology.fulfillment: Asaph twice mentions the rock, and it is the first proof of God's power that the people later forgot. Paul takes the rock as more than a source of water: 'they drank from the spiritual rock that accompanied them, and that rock was Christ,' 1 Corinthians 10:4. On the last day of the feast Jesus called out, 'If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink,' John 7:37. The correspondence is that the provision came from a struck, given source. It escalates because Christ is not a supply beside God's people but their life itself. Where the type falls short, the rock supplied a body's need; the water Christ gives becomes 'streams of living water,' John 7:38.

typology.type: Shiloh, the tent He had pitched among men, Psalm 78:60
typology.fulfillment: The tent at Shiloh was where God chose to dwell among Israel, and Asaph records that He abandoned it. John's Gospel says the Word 'made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14, using the language of tent-dwelling, and Jesus speaks of the 'temple of His body,' John 2:21. Shiloh shows that a place is only a sign; the true dwelling is a person. The type also bears a warning. When Jesus drove out the traders He quoted the same Jeremiah 7 that names Shiloh, Mark 11:17, and He foretold the fall of the temple, Matthew 24:2. The type falls short because Shiloh was abandoned, but the body of Christ, raised in three days, is not.

God passes over the tribe of the birthright and chooses Judah. Jacob had earlier promised that the scepter would not depart from Judah, Genesis 49:10, and the writer of Hebrews notes that 'our Lord descended from Judah,' Hebrews 7:14. In Revelation 5:5 the elder calls Him 'the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David.' The pattern of a chosen younger line finds its peak in the Messiah, who reigns from Zion. Yet the type is not a claim that any tribe deserves the honor. The psalm ties the choice to God's love alone, and in Christ the promise of Judah spills over to the nations.

typology.type: David taken from the sheepfolds, Psalm 78:70-72
typology.fulfillment: The shepherd-king is a promise that God will give His flock a leader after His own heart. Ezekiel 34:23 says God will appoint 'one shepherd, My servant David,' after the failure of the shepherds of Israel. Jesus claims that role by saying, 'I am the good shepherd,' John 10:11, and Hebrews calls Him 'that great Shepherd of the sheep,' Hebrews 13:20. David's integrity of heart was real but flawed, as 2 Samuel 11 shows. The correspondence falls short at that point, and Christ's shepherding has no such fracture: He lays down His life for the sheep rather than sparing it, John 10:15.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ by teaching. Matthew 13:34-35 presents Jesus' habit of speaking in parables as the fulfilment of Psalm 78:2. The link is more than a proof text. Asaph's parable told of God's works in the past and the hearts that resisted them. In Matthew 13:10-15 Jesus explains that His parables both reveal and conceal, so that hearers with hard hearts hear without understanding, quoting Isaiah. That is precisely the pattern the psalm traces in Israel: seeing wonders and not believing, verse 32. Jesus stands where Asaph stood, teaching a stubborn generation, but He speaks with the authority of the God whose works the psalm recounts.

It leads to Christ by the bread. The crowd who ate the loaves asked Him, 'What sign then will You perform, so that we may see it and believe You?' John 6:30, and then quoted 'He gave them bread from heaven to eat,' John 6:31. That is the wilderness scene of Psalm 78:18-25 played again: people fed by a miracle who still ask for proof. Jesus answers that it was not Moses who gave the bread but His Father who gives 'the true bread from heaven,' John 6:32. The manna fed a generation that died in the desert, while the true bread gives life to the world. The people's grumbling at Him, John 6:41, echoes the grumbling of the fathers.

It leads to Christ by the temple. Shiloh is the psalm's lesson that God will not be bound to a building. Jesus speaks in the same line as Jeremiah, quoting Jeremiah 7:11 as He cleanses the temple, Mark 11:17, and laments over Jerusalem, 'your house is left to you desolate,' Matthew 23:38. He then names Himself the temple that God will raise, John 2:19-21.

It leads to Christ by mercy that atones. Verse 38 says God forgave iniquity again and again. The New Testament says how He could do that and remain just: God presented Christ as the atoning sacrifice because 'in His forbearance He had passed over the sins committed beforehand,' Romans 3:25. The patience of Psalm 78 was not a loophole but a debt carried forward to the cross. And verse 39, God remembering that they were only flesh, finds its counterpart in the Son who took flesh, Hebrews 2:14, and who 'is able to sympathize with our weaknesses,' Hebrews 4:15.

Finally, it leads to Christ as Shepherd. Israel's kings did not all shepherd with integrity, and Ezekiel 34 says so. Micah 5:2-4 looks to a ruler from Bethlehem who will 'stand and shepherd His flock in the strength of the LORD.' Jesus comes as the Son of David, Matthew 1:1. A note of caution: David himself is not simply a picture of Christ, and the psalm does not say he is. The link runs through the promise, not through every detail of David's life.
study.god:
The first thing the psalm shows about God is His memory. Israel forgets, verses 11 and 42, and yet God remembers, verse 39, and does not let forgetfulness become the last word. The forgetting is not neutral. It is a slight against a Rescuer whose wonders were performed before their eyes. Asaph makes the point that the sin is to fail to keep in mind what the Lord has done.

He is a God of costly patience. Verse 38 sets a breathtaking sequence side by side: the people lie to Him with their tongues, and He is compassionate. The compassion is not sentimental. In verses 30 and 31 the anger burns while the meat is still in their mouths. The psalm holds the two together without smoothing them. He gave what they craved, verse 29, and the gift was itself a verdict, as Psalm 106:15 and Numbers 11:33 confirm. God's wrath is real, and it is measured; He does not rouse His full wrath, verse 38.

He is sovereign in election. He rejects the tent of Joseph, verse 67, and chooses Judah and Zion, 'which He loved,' verse 68. No reason is given but His love, as Deuteronomy 7:7-8 also insists for Israel as a whole. The choice of David makes the same point in a smaller frame, for the man chosen was found tending ewes, verse 71. God is free to raise the ordinary, and He does not need a strong candidate.

He is holy and He is jealous. The provocation of verse 58 is idolatry, and 'jealousy' is the language of a covenant partner who will not share His people. Yet He is also the Rock and Redeemer of verse 35, a name that ties the rescue to the very rock the people tested. And He is the shepherd, verse 52, who leads His flock safely, so that they do not fear.

The psalm also holds a tension it does not resolve. God abandons Shiloh and gives His strength into captivity, verse 61, yet He remains faithful to the flock. The way of both statements is that judgment falls on the sinful without cancelling the promise. The verse that says the Lord awoke, verse 65, is bold language, and Psalm 121:4 guards it, so that the picture is of the effect of His action and not of any sleep.

For worship, the psalm teaches us to recite God's works in the same breath as our failures, to bring children into that recitation, and to let mercy, not our record, be the reason we hope.

crossReferences.note: Matthew says Jesus' parables fulfil this psalm. Compare the wording: Matthew has 'hidden since the foundation of the world,' where the psalm has 'hidden from the beginning.' The evangelist reads the psalm as the announcement of a teacher who would speak the truth of Israel's story in a form only those with ears would grasp.

Moses charges Israel to guard against forgetting the things their eyes had seen and to teach them to their children and grandchildren. Psalm 78:4-7 is that command turned into a song, and its stated aim, trusting God and keeping His commands, matches the reason Moses gives.

The Song of the Sea looks ahead to the day God would lead His people to His holy dwelling, 'the mountain of Your inheritance.' Psalm 78:54-55 reads as its report: the promised leading and planting have happened. It also shows why the later losses hurt so much.

The narrative behind verses 26 to 31. A wind drives in the quail, the people gather them, and 'while the meat was still between their teeth' the plague strikes. The psalm strips the account to its moral point: God can give what a heart craves as judgment, and the graves are named for the craving.

God's own description of Himself after the golden calf. 'Compassionate and gracious, slow to anger' stands behind Psalm 78:38. The verse also says He will not leave guilt unpunished, which fits the psalm's balance of holding back anger in verse 38 and spending it in verses 30 to 31 and 59 to 64.

The historical event behind the loss of Shiloh. Israel is defeated, thirty thousand foot soldiers fall, and the ark of God is captured. Psalm 78:60-64 gives the theological verdict on it, that God Himself delivered His strength to captivity, and refuses to treat it as a mere military accident.

Centuries later Jeremiah tells the temple's defenders to go and look at Shiloh, 'where I first made a dwelling for My Name.' What happened there can happen to the house in which they trusted. Psalm 78 supplies the reasoning, that God takes no dwelling place for granted and owes no building its safety.

Psalm 106 tells the same wilderness and land history from the side of sin, and ends where Psalm 78 does, with rescue by God. 'Many times He rescued them' matches 'again and again' in Psalm 78:41. He 'remembered His covenant with them' answers Israel's forgetting.

Paul retells the wilderness generation with the sea, cloud, rock, craving and testing that Psalm 78 uses, and says these things 'took place as examples' for the church. He treats the history as living instruction, exactly as Asaph does.

God says to David, 'I took you from the pasture, from following the flock, to be the ruler over My people Israel.' It is the historical statement behind Psalm 78:70-71. The psalm makes the sheepfold the frame of the choice and the shepherding of a whole people its result.

After condemning Israel's false shepherds, God promises 'one shepherd, My servant David.' This is the prophetic hope that grows from Psalm 78:70-72, and it is the promise the New Testament sees fulfilled in the Son of David.

The writer quotes Psalm 95 on the wilderness generation who tested and tried God, and then warns the church against unbelief. Psalm 78:32 and 41 speak of the same failure, not believing despite the wonders, and Hebrews 4:1-2 applies it to those who hear the good news.

study.oneStory:
The psalm sits at one of the fault lines of the Bible's story: the point where a rescued people has been given everything and still does not trust. Creation's first question, whether human beings will believe God's word, shows up in Israel's wilderness, in the sneer 'Can God really prepare a table in the wilderness?' verse 19. It is the serpent's doubt again, now spoken by the redeemed.

Looking back, the psalm rests on the Exodus, which is the Old Testament's great act of redemption. It also recalls the promise of the land given to Abraham and the sea-song of Exodus 15. Looking forward, it sets up the rest of the Old Testament's story. The tent at Shiloh falls, the ark is captured, and the search for a faithful king and a place where God can dwell begins. Verses 65 to 72 answer in outline: God will choose Judah, Zion and David. That answer carries through the books of Samuel, the promise of an everlasting house in 2 Samuel 7, and the kingdom that later divides in 1 Kings 12.

The choice does not end the failure, and the prophets know it. Ezekiel 34 recalls that the shepherds also failed and promises that God Himself will rescue the flock and set 'one shepherd, My servant David' over it, Ezekiel 34:11-16 and 23. Micah 5:2-4 fixes the promise on a ruler from Bethlehem.

The New Testament tells us who that shepherd is. The Son of David comes teaching in the parables the psalm foretold, Matthew 13:35. He is the true bread from heaven, John 6:32, the temple of the body, John 2:21, and the good shepherd who lays down His life, John 10:11. He takes on Israel's failure by bearing its judgment, and He makes the forgiveness of verse 38 a righteous act, Romans 3:25-26.

The church, warned by the same history in 1 Corinthians 10:11, is now the flock that must not repeat the wilderness. And the end of the story is the answer to the psalm's deepest fear. Where Shiloh was abandoned and Israel's inheritance lost, the last book shows the dwelling of God with humanity, with no temple needed, and the Lamb as the shepherd of His people, Revelation 21:3 and 7:17.

sermon.title: Educating for Hope
sermon.why: Piper preaches directly from Psalm 78:1-8 on why God's people must teach the next generation His works so that they set their hope in God, the exact pastoral burden driving this psalm.

quiz.q: What is the psalm's stated purpose in verses 1-7?

options.text: To recount God's wonders so the next generation will set their hope in Him and not repeat their fathers' rebellion.
options.note: Verses 6-7 state this purpose explicitly.

options.text: To entertain the congregation with stories about Israel's past.
options.note: The psalm's aim is pastoral instruction, not entertainment.

options.text: To list Israel's kings for genealogical record.
options.note: The psalm recounts events and responses, not a genealogy.

options.text: To excuse Israel's disobedience as unavoidable.
options.note: The psalm names Israel's sin honestly rather than excusing it, though it does explain the pattern.

quiz.q: Despite the manna and quail God provided, how did Israel respond, verses 17-32?

options.text: They continued to test God and did not believe, even with the food still in their mouths.
options.note: Verses 30-32 describe judgment falling while the food was still being eaten.

options.text: They gave thanks briefly and then were satisfied forever.
options.note: Any gratitude was short-lived; the psalm stresses their continued unbelief.

options.text: They refused to eat the food God provided.
options.note: They ate eagerly, verse 29; the sin was ingratitude and unbelief, not refusal.

options.text: They never sinned again after being fed.
options.note: Verse 32 says plainly that in spite of all this they kept on sinning.

quiz.q: How does the psalm describe God's response to Israel's shallow, repeated unfaithfulness, verses 36-39?

options.text: He was compassionate, forgave their iniquity, and remembered they were but flesh, restraining His full wrath.
options.note: Verses 38-39 state this directly, even after naming their deceit in verses 36-37.

options.text: He ignored their sin as though it did not matter.
options.note: The psalm names their sin honestly rather than ignoring it.

options.text: He immediately and permanently destroyed the whole nation.
options.note: Judgment did fall at points, but the psalm stresses restraint, not total destruction.

options.text: He waited for them to earn forgiveness through good works.
options.note: The emphasis falls on God's own compassion and memory of their frailty, not on Israel earning anything.

quiz.q: What happened to the tabernacle at Shiloh, and why, verses 58-64?

options.text: God abandoned it and gave His people to the sword because they provoked Him with idols and high places.
options.note: Verses 58-62 tie the loss of Shiloh directly to Israel's idolatry.

options.text: It was peacefully relocated to Jerusalem by royal decree.
options.note: The psalm describes judgment and loss, not an orderly, peaceful transfer.

options.text: It was destroyed by a natural disaster unrelated to sin.
options.note: The text explicitly ties the loss to covenant unfaithfulness, not to an unrelated disaster.

options.text: It was rebuilt immediately afterward in the same location.
options.note: The psalm records loss and God's later choice of Zion instead, not a rebuilding at Shiloh.

quiz.q: Whom did God choose instead of Ephraim, and what does this anticipate, verses 67-72?

options.text: Judah, Zion, and David the shepherd king, anticipating Christ, the Son of David and the Good Shepherd.
options.note: Verses 68-72 name this choice, which the New Testament applies to Jesus.

options.text: Benjamin, anticipating Saul's kingship.
options.note: The psalm names Judah and David, not Benjamin or Saul.

options.text: No one; Ephraim continued to lead Israel afterward.
options.note: The text explicitly says God rejected Ephraim and chose Judah instead.

options.text: The Philistines, who then ruled over Israel.
options.note: The Philistines appear earlier as adversaries, not as God's chosen leadership for His people.

questions: The psalm exists so 'the next generation' would set their hope in God, verse 7. What are you doing, practically, to pass on God's works to those who come after you?
Israel forgot what God had done for them again and again, verse 11. What has God done for you that you are tempted to forget when new trials come?
Even when Israel's hearts were 'not loyal' and 'not faithful,' God 'was compassionate' and restrained His anger, verses 37-38. Where do you need to receive that same patient compassion today?
God chose the humble shepherd David over the more prominent tribe of Ephraim, verses 67-70. Where might you be tempted to trust in status rather than in God's sovereign, gracious choice?
David shepherded Israel 'with integrity of heart and skillful hands,' verse 72, a picture fulfilled in Jesus. How does knowing Christ is your perfect Shepherd change how you follow Him this week?

translationNotes.note: The phrase 'open my mouth in parables' and 'things hidden from the beginning' is quoted directly in Matthew 13:35 to explain why Jesus taught in parables, giving this verse a direct New Testament fulfillment.
The reason for Ephraim's retreat 'on the day of battle' is left unstated here; the following verses supply it by describing a pattern of forgetting God's covenant.
'The Lord awoke as from sleep' is a bold, figurative picture (an anthropomorphism) for God's sudden, decisive action to save; it does not mean God was ever literally inactive or asleep.
